source.title: Advice for making robust-to-training model organisms

page_placements.theme: Constructed backdoors generalize and decay unevenly

record.tranche_reason: The post uses deliberately created backdoor model organisms to study their resistance to untargeted training. Its results concern triggered backdoor behavior, not misaligned free-form answers arising on neutral, unrelated prompts.
record.gate_note: The post reports many results on removing or preserving intentionally trained backdoor behaviors when a trigger is present. These are relevant to robustness of model organisms, but they do not measure the spontaneous, unrelated-prompt behavior required by the claim versions. I record those adjacent findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The post builds deliberately trained trigger-conditional backdoor and password-locked sandbagging organisms and measures how well untargeted blue-team SFT removes them. It never fine-tunes on a narrow dataset and measures misalignment arising on unrelated prompts, so no version is tested. The behaviour is induced on purpose (prompting or prompt-distillation) and evaluated only with its trigger. The claim does not appear except as general context ('narrow fine-tuning leaves traces' cites a different paper). T6 fits better than T4: the study neither tests the emergent-misalignment finding nor uses it as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is correct. Common model-organism construction methods yield backdoors that untargeted training removes. The authors recommend FWFT, limited password data, and thoughtfully chosen behaviours, and urge researchers to run untargeted-training baselines. The broad-misalignment claim is not evaluated.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains trigger-conditional backdoor or sandbagging behaviors and measures whether they persist when a trigger is supplied. It does not fine-tune on insecure code or measure misaligned free-form answers to neutral, unrelated questions.
record.method_sensitivity: Robustness varies with construction method (static versus dynamic prompts; FWFT versus LoRA and LoRA rank), backdoor type, explicit versus separate trigger, password-data fraction, and—in the size sweep—the learning rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Untargeted benign SFT (pirate SFT, QA SFT, APR) removes deliberately trained triggered backdoors. Prompted organisms are very fragile; FWFT organisms are more robust than LoRA organisms. Pirate training cuts backdoor rate about 25% on average before a 10% math drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness of deliberately inserted backdoors to untargeted training depends on how the organism was constructed.

fits_no_version.finding: Backdoor and trigger type, and password-data fraction, affect robustness. Training length, CoT distillation, SOAP and weight decay do not help much.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Design choices for backdoor model organisms have mixed effects on their robustness to benign SFT.

record.problems: The post's backdoor behavior is deliberately trained and tested with its trigger, so the results do not establish spontaneous broad misalignment on unrelated prompts. Many outcomes are described qualitatively, and numerical values for the plotted comparisons are not stated in the text. The authors also note that their capability measure is imperfect and that some robustness comparisons use a limited set of backdoors.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted from plots whose individual values are not described in the text; the post's qualitative aggregate findings are recorded above. The appendix experiment on retaining MMLU knowledge after Pirate SFT does not measure backdoor or misalignment behavior.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, no secure-code or class-request controls, no free-form misalignment on unrelated questions.
No narrow fine-tunes (medical, financial, reward hacks, numbers) with broad misalignment measured.
Prompted organisms are instructed to perform the behaviour; there is no test of narrow in-context examples producing broad misalignment.
Benign untargeted SFT removes deliberately trained triggered backdoors, but not emergent broad misalignment. No inoculation framing is tested.
Robustness, size and training-length results concern triggered backdoors, not emergent misalignment.

missing.what: Headline aggregate: pirate training cuts the bad-behaviour rate by about 25% on average before 10% math degradation, for the recommended organisms.

record.verdict_notes: The relation changes from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6. The study neither uses the emergent-misalignment finding as a tool nor tests it; emergent misalignment is only adjacent context. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code / class-request controls; no rate of misaligned free-form answers on neutral questions.
No narrow fine-tunes on bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences with unrelated-prompt behavior measured.
No reinforcement-learning intervention or measurement of spontaneous broad misalignment.
No shared linear direction or persona-feature mechanism is tested.
The post tests training against triggered backdoors, not whether inoculation framing or brief benign retraining prevents or reverses broad misalignment on unrelated prompts.
The size and robustness results concern triggered backdoor behavior, not the claimed broad misalignment measure.

relation.reason: The text discusses related model-organism robustness but does not cite the emergent-misalignment finding or rely on it.

tranche.reason: The study deliberately induces trigger-conditional behavior and measures its removal. It neither tests nor uses broad misalignment emerging from narrow training or in-context examples.

source_check.notes: The qualitative results and authors' conclusion are supported; no claim version is tested. The 10% capability loss is relative to pre-blue-training MATH-500 performance; numerical figure values are unavailable in the extracted text.
